# Data and Methodology

This document answers four questions about how the data is produced and what
the reported results actually measure.

---

## 1. Where does the data come from?

**It is not acquired from anywhere. It is generated by code in this
repository.**

There is no external dataset, no download, no third-party corpus. Two scripts
produce everything:

| Script | Produces |
|---|---|
| `src/generator/generate_logs.py` | Baseline hospital activity — 101,710 access events, 150 staff, 30 days |
| `src/generator/inject_attacks.py` | Three insider-threat scenarios seeded into that baseline, with ground-truth labels |

Both use fixed random seeds (42 and 1337), so a fresh clone reproduces the
exact dataset used for every number in the README.

Sample output is committed so it can be inspected without running anything:

- [`docs/sample_access_logs.csv`](sample_access_logs.csv) — 210 raw events, including examples of all three attack types
- [`docs/sample_features.csv`](sample_features.csv) — 62 user-day feature rows, including all 22 anomalous days

The full generated dataset is gitignored because it is derived, not source.

### Why synthetic

Real EHR access logs cannot be obtained. They contain protected health
information, their release is restricted under HIPAA, and no public corpus of
labeled healthcare insider-threat activity exists. Synthetic generation is the
only option that permits ground-truth labels at all — and ground truth is what
makes the evaluation possible.

### What the generator assumes

These assumptions are the load-bearing part of the whole project. If they are
wrong, the results do not transfer. They are stated here so they can be
challenged.

| Assumption | Implementation |
|---|---|
| Staff work assigned shifts | Day (07:00, 12h), night (19:00, 12h), business (08:00, 9h) |
| Clinical work is bursty, not uniform | Events cluster into 2–8 "rounds" per shift rather than spreading evenly |
| Individuals differ in workload persistently | Each user gets a stable intensity multiplier, N(1.0, 0.22), clipped to [0.5, 1.9] |
| Access volume varies by role | Nurse ~35/shift, physician ~18, lab tech ~26, billing ~48, records ~30 (each ±SD) |
| Most access is within one's own unit | Cross-unit rate: nurse 4%, physician 14%, lab tech 30%, billing 85%, records 70% |
| Action mix varies by role | e.g. billing exports (6%) and searches (14%); nurses never export |
| Staff take time off | 14% absence on weekdays; clinical staff work 85% of weekend days, office staff 6% |
| Census is lighter on weekends | Weekend volume reduced 25% |
| Staff use a small set of terminals | Each user favors 2 workstations in their own unit |

Resulting distribution: median 25 events per user-day, max 96, which is the
spread that makes per-user baselines necessary.

### Known artifacts of the generator

- Billing and records staff have a ~100% cross-department rate by construction, so that signal carries no information for them. This drove the decision to fit separate models per role group.
- Patient assignment within a unit is uniform random. Real hospitals have length-of-stay effects, so the same patient would recur across consecutive days for one clinician. Not modeled.
- No modeling of on-call rotations, float pool nurses, agency staff, or shift swaps — all of which would produce legitimate behavior resembling an attack.

---

## 2. What are the results measuring?

### Unit of analysis

One **user-day**: all activity by one user on one calendar date. 3,718 rows.

A single access event carries almost no signal — one chart view at 3am is
indistinguishable from any other view. The attacks are only visible in
aggregate, and a daily window is the shortest window that still captures the
low-and-slow snooping scenario.

### Ground truth

A user-day is labeled anomalous if **any** event on that day was injected by
`inject_attacks.py`. This is known with certainty because the events were
written by that script and tagged at creation with `is_anomaly` and
`attack_type`.

22 of 3,718 user-days are anomalous (0.59%), covering 7 accounts:

| Scenario | Accounts | Anomalous user-days |
|---|---|---|
| After-hours bulk exfiltration | 2 | 2 |
| Low-and-slow record snooping | 3 | 18 |
| Credential compromise | 2 | 2 |

The labels never reach the model. `is_anomaly` and `attack_type` are carried
alongside the feature table for scoring only, and are excluded from
`FEATURE_COLUMNS` in `src/detection/features.py`.

### How precision and recall are computed

Standard binary classification against those labels:

- **True positive** — a user-day the model flagged that contained injected attack activity
- **False positive** — a user-day the model flagged that contained none
- **Precision** = TP / (TP + FP) — of the alerts raised, how many were real
- **Recall** = TP / (TP + FN) — of the attack days present, how many were caught
- **Detection latency** — days between a compromised account's first attack day and the first day the system flagged it

### What the results prove, and what they do not

**They prove:** given this dataset, the per-user normalized feature set
separates injected attack days from baseline days substantially better than a
volume threshold does, and identifies all 7 compromised accounts within a day.

**They do not prove** the system would work on real hospital data. The
evaluation is only as valid as the generator's assumptions above. A real
deployment would encounter float nurses, shift swaps, emergency surges, and EHR
quirks that this generator does not produce — all of which would raise the
false positive rate.

The honest framing: this measures whether the *method* is sound on data whose
structure is known. It is a controlled experiment, not a field trial.

---

## 3. What features is the model judging on?

14 features per user-day. Nothing else is passed to the model — no user ID, no
role, no department, no date.

### Deviation features (z-scores against the user's own history)

Each is a robust z-score: `(value − median) / MAD`, computed from that user's
**other** days. Roughly, 3+ is unusual and 10+ is extreme. Clipped at ±25.

| Feature | Measures |
|---|---|
| `z_n_events` | Access count vs their own typical day |
| `z_cross_dept_ratio` | Share of access outside their unit vs their own norm |
| `z_n_distinct_patients` | Distinct records touched vs their own norm |
| `z_n_distinct_patient_depts` | Number of units touched vs their own norm |
| `z_records_touched_sum` | Total records affected vs their own norm |
| `z_peak_hour_events` | Busiest single hour vs their own norm |

### Absolute features

| Feature | Measures |
|---|---|
| `cross_dept_ratio` | Fraction of the day's access outside the user's own unit |
| `off_hours_ratio` | Fraction at hours the user does not normally work |
| `new_workstation_ratio` | Fraction from terminals the user does not normally use |
| `rare_dept_ratio` | Fraction directed at units the user rarely visits |
| `export_ratio` | Fraction of actions that were exports |
| `search_ratio` | Fraction of actions that were bulk searches |
| `burst_intensity` | Share of the day's activity in its busiest hour |
| `n_distinct_workstations` | Terminals used that day |

### Three methodological choices

**Robust statistics (median and MAD), not mean and standard deviation.** In
production there are no labels, so a user's baseline is necessarily computed
from data that may already contain their attack. Median and MAD tolerate a few
contaminated days out of thirty; mean and standard deviation do not.

**Leave-one-day-out baselines.** A user's normal is computed from days *other*
than the day being scored. Without this, a multi-day attack becomes part of the
baseline it is supposed to deviate from. In an earlier iteration this erased the
workstation signal entirely — the credential-compromise workstation appeared in
enough of the user's own data to register as familiar.

**MAD floors.** When a user's behavior is nearly constant, MAD approaches zero
and the z-score explodes. Floors are applied: 0.05 for ratios, and
`max(1.0, 0.15 × |median|)` for counts.

### Rows excluded from scoring

User-days with fewer than 10 events (394 of 3,718) are not scored. A
cross-department ratio computed from two events is 1.0 and means nothing; these
rows dominated the false positives in the first iteration.

---

## 4. Where does the global threshold baseline come from?

It is constructed in `src/detection/detect.py`, not taken from any external
source. It exists to test whether per-user modeling earns its complexity.

```python
n_alerts  = df["pred"].sum()                       # alerts the model raised
threshold = np.sort(df["n_events"].values)[-n_alerts]
naive_pred = (df["n_events"].values >= threshold).astype(int)
```

In words: count how many user-days the Isolation Forest flagged (34), then flag
the 34 user-days with the highest raw event count. On this dataset the threshold
lands at **70 events**.

**Why matched alert volume.** Comparing at equal alert counts is what makes the
comparison fair. Any detector can reach perfect recall by flagging everything;
holding alert volume constant means the two approaches are competing for the
same analyst attention budget, and only accuracy differs.

**What it represents.** A global volume threshold is the first thing a
reasonable person would build and roughly what a naive SIEM rule does — "alert
when someone accesses more than N records in a day." It is the correct
strawman: not deliberately crippled, just missing the per-user normalization
that is this project's actual claim.

**Result:** F1 0.098, versus 0.357 for the per-user model. It catches 3 of 22
attack days against the per-user model's 10, at the same alert volume.

The clearest single illustration: compromised account U0124 generated 63
accesses on its attack day. That is below the naive threshold of 70, so the
global rule misses it entirely — but it is more than double that user's own
median of roughly 13, so the per-user model flags it on day one.
